props.title: Tales of Manhattan

sections.content: Tales of Manhattan (1942) pioneered the multi-narrative anthology format, following a cursed tailcoat as it passes between owners and ruins lives. This groundbreaking structure influenced later episodic films like Dead Reckoning (1947) and The Yellow Rolls-Royce (1964). Director Julien Duvivier assembled an incredible cast including Charles Boyer, Rita Hayworth, Henry Fonda, and Paul Robeson, using the coat as a device to explore class divisions, moral corruption, and redemption across New York's social strata.

sections.content: The anthology format flourished in 1940s Hollywood, with films like Flesh and Fantasy (1943) and Quartet (1948) building on Tales of Manhattan's framework. These films used objects or locations as narrative threads, creating interconnected stories that examined society from multiple angles. The format reached its artistic peak with La Ronde (1950), Max Ophüls' masterful exploration of love and desire across social classes.

The film's examination of class mobility through clothing was revolutionary, predating similar themes in All About Eve (1950) and The Man in the White Suit (1951). The tailcoat becomes both status symbol and burden, revealing how appearances shape identity in American society. Paul Robeson's final segment, though controversial for its stereotypical elements, provided rare screen time for African American performers in 1940s Hollywood. sections.content: Modern anthology films like Paris, je t'aime (2006) and New York, I Love You (2008) owe a debt to Tales of Manhattan's innovative structure. The film established key anthology conventions: thematic unity, symbolic connecting devices, and social commentary through multiple perspectives. Director Duvivier's technique of using match cuts and thematic echoes between segments influenced later anthology masters like Robert Altman in Short Cuts (1993).
